text.p: A decision is expected soon in the bitter legal battle between Seagram Co Ltd and Viacom Inc over their USA Network joint partnership agreement.

In early February, at the end of a 19 day trial and post- trial briefing, Vice Chancellor Myron Steele of the Delaware Chancery Court told both sides he hoped to have a decision in 90 days. A court spokeswoman will not say when the decision is due but advises reporters to "call back next week."

At issue is Seagram's allegation that Viacom's 1996 launch of "Nick at Nite TV Land" on Nickelodeon network and its ongoing ownership of the MTV network violate a clause in the partnership agreement that bars either partner from owning a competing cable operation.

The partnership was originally formed in 1981 by Time Warner Inc and Paramount Communications Inc predecessor Gulf & Western Industries Inc, and was soon joined by MCA Inc. Viacom became a USA Network partner with its acquisition of Paramount in 1994 and Seagram with its acquisition of 80 percent of MCA Inc in 1995.

In a countersuit, Viacom contends that the partnership is working fine and that its MTV and Nickelodeon networks are grandfathered in. It further alleges in court papers that Seagram's lawsuit seeking a court order compelling Viacom to sell its USA stake is a violation of antitrust laws.

When the trial on both lawsuits began in October, Seagram was reported to have agreed to sell its stake to Viacom for $1.7 billion in cash and assets. In testimony, Seagram chief Edgar Bronfman implied the deal fell through because of his reluctance to pay the related high tax bill.
Also called as witnesses in the trial were Viacom chairman Sumner Redstone and former studio executives who had participated in the early partnership negotiations.
A report published Friday in the Wall Street Journal said that MCA's Universal Studios is now interested in buying Viacom's half of the partnership.
But a reliable source told Reuters "There are no negotiations. Somebody's trying to make something happen."
A second independent source said "Don't assume there are any negotiations going on."

A Delaware attorney unrelated to the case but with an extensive practice in corporate and contract law told Reuters "These people are crazy not to settle if they want control over their destinies. By throwing such a mixture of claims on the table they have no way of knowing how the court will come out. To the extent that what we are talking about here is economics rather than egos, rationality would suggest that the parties reach a negotiated solution," the attorney said.
Attorneys and spokespersons for both sides declined to comment.
